COMPSCI 61A 001 - LEC 001 offered through Electrical Engineering and Computer Sciences
section closed

The Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs

Kay Ousterhout
Jan 19, 2027 - May 07, 2027
Mo, We, Fr
01:00 pm - 01:59 pm
Dwinelle 155
Class #:28320
Units:4

Instruction Mode: In-Person Instruction

Time Conflict Enrollment Allowed

Open Seats

173 Unreserved Seats

An introduction to programming and computer science focused on abstraction techniques as means to manage program complexity. Techniques include procedural abstraction; control abstraction using recursion, higher-order functions, generators, and streams; data abstraction using interfaces, objects, classes, and generic operators; and language abstraction using interpreters and macros. The course exposes students to programming paradigms, including functional, object-oriented, and declarative approaches. It includes an introduction to asymptotic analysis of algorithms. There are several significant programming projects.

#27054
DUTCH 161AC 001 - LEC 001 offered through German
section closed

Multiracial Americans: The History and future of racially-mixed communities in the United States

Jeroen Dewulf
Jan 19, 2027 - May 07, 2027
Tu, Th
02:00 pm - 03:29 pm
Moffitt Library 101
Class #:27054
Units:4

Instruction Mode: In-Person Instruction

No Open Seats
In this course, we study three multiracial communities with a Dutch-American connection, one that identifies as African American, one as Native American and one as Asian American, and take these cases as a point of departure for a broader discussion on the history and future of racially-mixed people in American society. This focus is important considering that people of mixed race have experienced a long history of discrimination in the United States. Racial mixture was long associated with degeneration, and racial theorists claimed that it weakened physical, intellectual and moral qualities such as strength, endurance, honesty, and even fertility.

COMPSCI 294 137 - LEC 137 offered through Electrical Engineering and Computer Sciences
section closed

Special Topics

Immersive Computing and Virtual Reality
Allen Y Yang
Jan 19, 2027 - May 07, 2027
Mo, We
02:00 pm - 03:29 pm
The Gateway Building B1022
Class #:33914
Units:3

Instruction Mode: In-Person Instruction

Open Seats

This graduate course examines the foundations and applications of augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and immersive computing. Students connect human perception with the hardware, computer vision, and interaction techniques that support immersive experiences, while learning to evaluate existing technologies and develop solutions that address users’ needs. Topics include visual and multisensory perception, 3D displays, depth cameras, perspective projection, marker-based tracking, and structure from motion. The course also explores 3D input devices, speech and language interfaces, user orientation and movement, virtual identity, and inclusive design, alongside developments in artificial intelligence and hardware acceleration. Programming assignments provide experience with Unity3D, AR/VR application development, smartphone deployment, and computer vision. A final project brings together background research, prototyping, progress reviews, presentations, and a written report. By the end of the course, students should be able to critically assess AR/VR hardware and software and design and implement immersive applications informed by technical capabilities and human needs. Students should have programming proficiency in C, C++, or C#, with preparation comparable to CS 61A and CS 61B.

#17425
COMPSCI 294 279 - LEC 279 offered through Electrical Engineering and Computer Sciences
section closed

Special Topics

Measuring and Improving the Societal Impacts of AI
Emma Pierson
Jan 19, 2027 - May 07, 2027
Mo, We
03:30 pm - 04:59 pm
The Gateway Building B1026
Class #:17425
Units:3

Instruction Mode: In-Person Instruction

Open Seats

AI is hurtling forward — but is that a good thing? This course will give you tools for measuring the societal impacts of AI, and shaping them for the better. First, we will discuss how to monitor the impacts of AI on diverse domains, including employment, education, social relationships, mental health, and cybersecurity. Second, we will discuss techniques for creating trustworthy and reliable AI systems. Finally, we will examine case studies using AI to concretely improve people’s lives (with examples drawn from healthcare, social inequality, and other domains). The class will feature numerous guest speakers from academia, journalism, non-profits, and industry. The main course assignments will consist of reading, presenting, and analyzing technical papers and popular press articles, along with a final project.

Special Topics

Cryptographic Computer Systems
Henry Corrigan-Gibbs, Sanjam Garg
Jan 19, 2027 - May 07, 2027
Tu, Th
09:30 am - 10:59 am
The Gateway Building B1012
Class #:17436
Units:3

Instruction Mode: In-Person Instruction

Open Seats

This graduate course will study systems that use cryptography to protect their users' privacy and security. We will have a lively in-class discussion each meeting of the class about a different topic on this theme. To prepare for those discussions, students will read 3-4 research papers each week -- a mix of recent papers and classic ones. Topics may include: AI security (watermarking, model stealing, private inference, ...), cryptographic protocols (oblivious RAM, private information retrieval, ...) and case studies of deployed systems (Private Cloud Compute, private telemetry, encrypted messaging, ...). The enrolled students and current events will largely determine the topics that we will cover. Over the course of the semester, students will pursue their own small research project; the deliverables will be a short technical write-up of their system and a complete open-source software artifact.

#17438
COMPSCI 294 312 - LEC 312 offered through Electrical Engineering and Computer Sciences
section closed

Special Topics

Proof Complexity and Modern Applications
Jan 19, 2027 - May 07, 2027
Tu
03:00 pm - 05:59 pm
Class #:17438
Units:3

Instruction Mode: In-Person Instruction

Open Seats

Proof complexity studies the following question: Given a true mathematical statement, what is the length of the shortest proof that the statement is true and how difficult is it to find a proof? Proof complexity is fundamentally connected both to major open questions of computational complexity theory and to practical properties of automated theorem provers and reasoning systems. Moreover, new connections between proof complexity and circuit complexity have been uncovered, and the interplay between these two areas has become quite rich. In addition, concepts and techniques in proof complexity have borrowed from and contributed to several other areas of computer science, including: cryptography, automated reasoning and AI, complexity of search classes within NP, the analysis of heuristics and algorithms for NP-hard problems, and bounded arithmetic. In the last 10–15 years, enormous progress has been made in proof complexity, with many open problems resolved, and many promising directions to attack other problems. For example, recent work (that we will cover) uses proof complexity to achieve breakthrough lower bounds on locally decodable codes, as well as the development of algorithms for a variety of distributional learning problems through the “Sum of Squares” paradigm. This course is intended to serve as an introduction to modern proof complexity, emphasizing its connections with computational complexity and algorithms in optimization. We will also discuss current research for speeding up theorem proving and verification that combine powerful tools from proof complexity, theorem proving and generative AI.

60 Unreserved Seats

This is a course for aspiring Academic Interns (AIs). It provides pedagogical training and guidance to students by introducing them to the Big Ideas of Teaching and Learning, and how to put them into practice. The course covers what makes a safe learning environment, how students learn, how to guide students toward mastery, and psychosocial factors that can negatively affect even the best students and best teachers. Class covers both theoretical and practical pedagogical aspects of teaching STEM subjects—specifically Computer Science. An integral feature of the course lies in the weekly AI experience that students perform to practice their teaching skills.

This course provides a graduate-level introduction to Natural Language Processing (NLP). We will survey foundational approaches such as word representations and n-gram language models, followed by neural methods including recurrent networks and attention mechanisms, and then progress to modern Transformer-based architectures. In addition, the course will cover advanced topics in contemporary NLP, including retrieval-augmented models, mixture-of-experts architectures, AI agents, and memorization.
